Nordea third-quarter results 2025

16.10.2025 klo 10.00

Nordea Bank

Ilkka Unknown

00:37 - 01:09

Good morning and welcome to Nordea's third quarter 2025 results.

I'm Ilkka, head of investor relations. As usual, we'll start with a presentation by Group CEO Frank Vang-Jensen, followed by a Q&A session with Frank and Group CFO Ian Smith.

Please remember to dial into the teleconference to ask questions. With that, Frank, please go ahead. Good morning.

Frank Vang-Jensen

01:10 - 20:05

Today, we have published our results for the third quarter of 2025. Again, it was a very solid quarter for Nordea. The past few months have reminded us that the world economy is delicately balanced. Political shifts and rising global tensions indicate that the operating environment can change quickly. Still, after the turbulent first few months of the year, the third quarter felt more calm and settled.

Some of the earlier uncertainty around tariffs receded when the new EU-US trade agreement was struck.

The Nordic economies also continued to benefit from low inflation and interest rates, conditions that helped lift confidence during the quarter.

Nordea Corporate signaled a renewed appetite to invest.

That translated into increased demand for lending.

Household activity also showed clear signs of picking up. Lending demand was still at muted levels while customers' main focus was on growing their savings. We also saw continued activity in investments. In this environment,

Nordea delivered higher business volumes and very solid results.

Our performance again demonstrated the strength and quality of our pan-Nordic business. Looking at some of the highlights for Q3, our return on equity was strong at 15.8%, in line with our financial target. We have now delivered a return on equity of above 15% in ten out of the past 11 quarters.

Earnings per share were €0.36. Mortgage lending increased by 6% and retail deposits were up 8%, supported by our business in Norway and Sweden.

Corporate lending grew by 6% year on year and deposits were up 1%.

Assets under management were up 11% to €456 billion. Total income remained resilient, decreasing by 3%.

As expected, net interest income was lower following the policy rate reductions, decreasing by 6% year on year and by 1% quarter on quarter. Net fee and commission income was up 5%, rebounding after the market volatility seen in the previous quarters. Net insurance results grew by 10%. Net fair value result was in line with our expectations and fairly typical for the quarter. However, it was down 14% when compared with the unusually high level a year ago. Costs were stable year on year and quarter on quarter, supported by stabilized investment levels and careful management of headcounts. Full year operating expenses are expected to be around €5.4 billion and well within our guided range.

The cost-to-income ratio with amortized resolution fees was 46.1%. Operating profit was €1.6 billion, 2% lower than a year ago and stable quarter on quarter. Our credit and asset quality remain exceptionally strong. Net loan losses and similar net result amounted to a net reversal of €19 million this quarter.

We released a further €50 million from our management judgment buffer.

The release was driven by strong credit quality, reduced uncertainty, and lower credit risk due to lower rates and inflation.

Our strong capital generation continued and, at the end of September, our CET1 ratio was 15.9%.

That put us two to three percentage points above the current regulatory requirement. Today, we announced that we will shortly launch a new €250 million share buy-back program, in line with our commitment to regularly trim excess capital and return it to our shareholders.

All part of maintaining an efficient capital structure.

Our 2025 outlook is unchanged.

We are well on track to meet our guidance for the full year.

That is a return on equity of above 15%.

With that summary, let's now take a closer look at the results, starting with the income lines.

Net interest income remained resilient in the lower interest rate environment.

Our net interest income was supported by both higher lending and deposit volumes, along with the contribution from our deposit hedge. The deposit hedge contributed positively to our income in the quarter, increasing NII by €127 million year on year. Our net interest margin for the quarter was 1.59%. This compares with 1.64% last quarter and 1.77% a year ago. 77 a year ago.

The difference was due mainly to lower deposit and equity margins, as expected, given the policy rate reductions. Mortgage lending grew by 6%, driven by strong growth in Sweden and our Norwegian acquisition.

Excluding the acquisition, mortgage lending was up 1%, and corporate lending was strong, increasing further by 6%. Retail deposits were up 8% while corporate deposits were up 1%.

Net fee and commission income increased by 5% year on year, supported by growth in all our main lines.

The higher savings fee income was driven by higher assets under management, with positive net flows in all channels.

In our Nordic channels, we had strong net flows of €4.4 billion, driven by continued strong performance in private banking and our life and pension business.

Net flows from international channels were €0.6 billion, with net positive flows of €0.4 billion in wholesale distribution, brokerage, and advisory fee income. Income improved this quarter, driven by higher debt capital markets activity. Net fair value result was solid for the quarter, although it was lower compared to the unusually high figure from a year ago. We benefited from good levels of customer activity in a seasonally soft quarter, especially in foreign exchange and interest rate hedging products and our markets.

The result was strong.

Costs in the third quarter were stable year on year. That development reflects our strategic investments in technology and other key areas, leveling off as planned.

It also comes from our usual cost discipline.

We continue to actively manage our costs according to the operating environment, and headcount is lower. Looking at the full year 2025, our expectation is that operating expenses will be around €5.4 billion, which is slightly better than previously anticipated.

The third-quarter cost-to-income ratio was 46.1%, unchanged from the second quarter. Our credit quality continues to be exceptionally strong, which has resulted in net loan losses and a similar net result for Q3 being favorable, amounting to a reversal of €19 million.

Loan loss provisions and write-offs have been low, well below the long-term average, stemming from customers' stable financial positions, as well as our diversification and prudent credit policies. Given the lower provisioning requirements and the continued strength of our credit portfolio. We have released the first €50 million from our Management judgement buffer.

The buffer now stands at €291 million, compared with €341 million in Q2 and €435 million a year ago. Our capital position is strong, supported by continued robust capital generation.

At the end of the quarter, our CET1 ratio was 15.9%, 2.3 percentage points above the current regulatory requirement. We continue to use share buybacks to secure an efficient capital structure and focus on shareholder returns. Our next €250 million buyback program will be our fourth this year.

We will launch it on or around the 20th of October.

Let us then turn to our business areas and personal banking. We delivered solid business volumes. Customer activity increased during the quarter, especially in savings and investments. This was visible in the strong growth in deposits, up 8% year on year.

Many customers still feel somewhat uncertain about global developments. However, there are signs that confidence is improving.

This was visible in higher activity in the housing markets, although the pace is still slow.

We saw a further increase in demand for loan promises and mortgage lending increased by 6% year on year.

Here, growth was driven by Sweden and Norway. Excluding our Norwegian acquisition, mortgage lending was up 1%.

Households also continued to put money into investment funds.

Net flows in our Nordic retail funds were €0.7 billion during the quarter. Demand for our digital services remained high.

App users and logins grew by 6% and 8%, respectively. We also received more external recognition in this area, winning Best Nordic Digital Bank in both the Euromoney and Global Finance Awards.

The work we have done in digital has really moved us forward and means we have some of the best digital services in Europe today. Total income decreased by 3%, driven by lower policy rates. The decrease was partly offset by the higher income from payment cards and savings return on allocated equity.

With a modernized resolution, fees were 16%. The cost-to-income ratio was 52%.

In business banking, we performed well and delivered volume growth supported by higher customer activity.

Demand for lending grew in all markets, led by Sweden and Norway, which showed increased confidence among our small and medium-sized business customers who continue to settle into the new operating environment.

Lending volumes overall increased by 5%.

Deposits were up 9% year on year.

Also, with growth across all Nordic countries, our investments in developing our customer experience and digital capabilities are clearly resonating with our SME customers. We performed well in the annual EPC industry survey, improving our customer satisfaction results relative to peers across all markets. In Sweden, we achieved the highest rating among peer institutions.

We also received external recognition for our digital offering for SMEs, winning the titles of Best Corporate Digital Bank and Best Mobile Banking App in the Global Finance Awards.

Total income for Q3 was down 5% year-on-year, driven by lower rates and net interest income.

The decrease was partly offset by the higher net fee and commission income, where we had higher income from lending fees and debt.

Capital markets return on allocated equity improved with a strong margin, highlighting our resolution capabilities.

Fees were 16%. The cost-to-income ratio was 46%.

In the last quarter, institutions. We continued to use our expertise, Nordea scale and strong balance sheet to support our customers with their investment and growth plans, even as broader market uncertainty persists.

Nordic large caps continue to be cautiously optimistic in their outlook.

We saw a pick-up in event-driven transactions and related financing, and robust demand for additional liquidity. This was evident in the strong demand for lending, as our volumes increased by 6% year on year, up from 4%. Growth in Q2 deposits decreased by 7% year on year. This was mainly driven by a few larger customers in Denmark and Norway. Debt capital markets activity remained high, with broader-based transaction volumes among both corporate and institutional customers. During the quarter, we arranged more than 120 transactions.

That makes it more than 500 for the year to date and reinforces our leading position in the DCM space.

One of the highlights of the quarter was a green bond for the Kingdom of Denmark, valued at 7 billion Danish crowns.

Market conditions remained volatile for equity capital markets and mergers and acquisitions.

However, several M&A transactions were announced and ECM activity showed signs of recovery.

Social income was resilient, decreasing by 2% due to the rate reductions.

Net fee and commission income was up 4% due to event-driven business.

Return on equity was 16% and the cost-to-income ratio was 41%.

In asset and wealth management. We drove solid business momentum in our private banking, and investment performance was strong.

We continued to perform very well in private banking with €1.5 billion of net flows. The third quarter is typically quieter on account of the holiday period.

However, customer activity was at a record high.

We were very proactive towards our private banking customers through our advisors and across various special events. During the quarter in Sweden, we drove high investment activity, including helping our customers take part in several IPOs across the Nordics.

The steadier markets and more positive sentiment also helped.

After the volatility of spring and early summer in our international channels, net flows were positive as well, amounting to €0.6 billion. Wholesale distribution continued to stabilize, contributing €0.4 billion of that, with the remainder from international institutions. Net flows in life and pension were €1.2 billion, which was a record high gross written premium.

Premiums amounted to €2.9 billion, compared with €2.6 billion a year ago. As of year-end, the assets under management increased by 11% year on year to 456 billion, driven by the positive flows and strong market performance. We were pleased to see strong interest in our new Empower Europe fund that invests in the drivers of Europe's transformation, energy resilience, reshoring, and defense and cybersecurity.

Total income declined by 1% during the quarter, primarily due to a decrease in net interest and net fair value income. Net fee and commission income was up 1%, driven by higher assets under management.

Return on allocated equity was 33%.

The cost-to-income ratio was 44%. In summary, this was not a good quarter for Nordea. We are well on track to deliver on our target of a full-year return on equity of above 15%. Our performance so far this year clearly highlights our strength, strong customer focus, and our highly profitable and well-diversified pan-Nordic business model, along with our scale and efficiency. Nordea also has the advantage of operating in the Nordic markets, all of which are globally competitive, innovative, resilient, low-risk, and highly digital. All that makes the Nordics well equipped to navigate the current global shifts. Finally, we have our Capital Markets Day in London coming up on the 5th of November.

We look forward to presenting our plans and financial targets for our next strategy period.

We will share the concrete steps we are taking to build on our successful foundation, with a continued focus on our four home markets. These will enable us to drive above-market business growth with improved cost efficiency through our Nordea scale.

They will also be positioned to continue delivering market-leading return on equity and achieve superior earnings per share growth. We are well on track to deliver on our target of a full-year return on equity of above 15%.

Ilkka Unknown

20:28 - 20:37

Operator. We're now ready to take the questions, and as a courtesy to others, just a reminder if you can limit yourself to a maximum of two questions, please.

We are well on track to deliver on our target of a full year return on equity of above 15%.

Operator

20:43 - 21:10

If you wish to ask a question, please dial the Pound Key and five on your telephone keypad to enter the queue. If you wish to withdraw your question, please press the Pound Key on your telephone keypad. The next question comes from Andreas Hakanson from SEB. Please go ahead.

Andreas Hakanson

21:16 - 21:39

Good morning, everyone. So let's skip the personnel questions for now. And can we just start with you talking about the recovery in activity levels towards the end of the quarter? Could you tell us a little bit about where you see those activities picking up, in which segments and countries? If you can talk about your outlook a little bit into Q4 and maybe even for 2026?

That's my first question.

Ian Smith

21:42 - 23:34

Morning, Andre. Sorry, I was waiting for your second one there as well. Good morning. It's Ian here. It was certainly a good pickup towards the end of the quarter. July and August are traditionally quieter given seasonality, but seemed quieter than usual. The key things that we saw coming through again in September.

At the end of Q3, there was strong demand for corporate lending. So fairly evenly split across Business Banking and large corporates.

There was some recovery in our corporate activity levels, which helped to drive fees and then reflected a good market performance. That helped with AuM.

We also saw good flows coming through, particularly in the Nordic channels.

So, life and pensions, and private banking.

So fairly broad-based both on the corporate lending side and on activity levels that drove fees.

Now, the weaker spot is the mortgage market, as we all know. Although Sweden is reasonably active and we performed extremely well there, other markets are still pretty slow. I guess Norway has some good activity levels, so more muted on housing, but I'd say corporate-led. We'd like to see that momentum sustained into Q4. But as we've seen throughout this year, things are generally quite finely balanced, though I think we go into Q4 with a genuine sense of momentum.

And we hope that'll continue to build slowly into 2026.

Andreas Hakanson

23:36 - 24:02

At the end of Q3, there was strong demand for corporate lending. And then, I mean, I booked my flight ticket to London, so I don't want you to front-run the whole Capital Markets day. But if we look at the number of FTEs, they're falling quite nicely now in the last two quarters.

Frank Vang-Jensen

24:03 - 24:33

Hi Andreas, this is Frank speaking.

I will say that we will come back to this question in two and a half weeks. But what you see this year is that we have adjusted our cost base to the environment somewhat, so it's not a big change. But of course, you should expect us to continuously become even more efficient. So let's come back to that topic.

Andreas Hakanson

24:34 - 24:36

At the end of Q3, there was strong demand for corporate lending. At the end of Q3, there was strong demand for corporate lending. That's it.

Operator

24:42 - 24:48

The next question comes from Marcus Sandgren from Kepler Cheuvreux.

Please go ahead.

Marcus Sandgren

24:54 - 25:04

Good morning everyone. So just following up on Andreas' question, how about the sentiment in Finland? It seems to be struggling a bit.

That's my first question.

Frank Vang-Jensen

25:04 - 26:25

Let me take that one. So yes, Finland is a more stable country. And I think that is built on cultural reasons, but also historical and natural reasons. So a more stable, more cautious but very profitable and a very solid country to run a bank in.

Right now there is a somewhat gloomy view, but it is being addressed. The government is, in my view, doing the right things to get the economy back on track by lowering costs and lowering taxes to increase growth. And although it goes slowly, I do sense that the trend is upwards now when it comes to sentiment and also the confidence in the future. But there is a slight tendency to talk down the country and that's a cultural thing.

But people are aware of it. So let's see when it comes to the substance; actually, people are paying the bill. They have a lot of liquidity.

It's just sitting. A slight lack of confidence. So let's see how it will develop. I'm not that skeptical. Nor am I that negative. It is that Finland has what it takes.

Marcus Sandgren

26:27 - 27:02

Okay, good. And then secondly, on asset quality, it seems like you're really delivering well there. And you're still reiterating that you want to release this management buffer gradually. What kind of risks are you considering? I mean, is it just because you don't want to distribute it all in one quarter? Or is there anything related to risk because it seems like your underlying asset quality is much better. And we're through the rate hike cycle. And most of these effects should be visible now.

So what's the reason to keep it more than to just be gradual in releasing it? Thanks.

Ian Smith

27:03 - 28:11

So, Markus, it's Ian here. Yeah. You're right. The portfolio's performing extremely well.

All of the leading indicators, as well as the actual level of loan losses being low, are pretty strong. I guess we're a bank that moves with caution. It is harder to find reasons to hold on to additional buffers given the strength of the portfolio. And we've always been fairly clear that we'll either use it if we need it or release it. So, I and we have further said in the past that we wouldn't expect it to still be with us, certainly by the end of 2026.

So, we'll continue to stay close to what's happening in the portfolio. And if we continue to see the strengthening that we've seen throughout this year, it'll be hard to hold on to that management buffer.

Marcus Sandgren

28:12 - 28:23

Oh. Very well. Okay, thanks. And then there's no reason to change the outlook of ten basis points losses through the cycle. At least not for the coming two and a half weeks.

Ian Smith

28:23 - 28:36

No. However, it's a question that comes up quite often. So, we will talk about that a bit more on the 5th of November, but no changes.

Marcus Sandgren

28:37 - 28:38

The portfolio's performing extremely well. Very good.

The portfolio's performing extremely well.

Operator

28:43 - 28:49

The next question comes from Martin Ekstedt from Handelsbanken. Please go ahead.

Martin Ekstedt

28:54 - 29:37

Hello. Good morning and thank you for taking my questions. Firstly, I listened to Ian speaking at a conference between quarters regarding the Danish business, which is currently a preoccupation. We've discussed the Finnish business previously.

Right.

But now you stopped reporting on a country basis more than a decade ago. So I just wanted to check if you could share some more detail on what this preoccupation has been about, what you've been focused on, what the underlying cause was, perhaps, and if this turned positive in the right direction in Q3.

The portfolio's performing extremely well. That's the first one.

Ian Smith

29:37 - 31:26

Yes. Hi, Martin.

Yes. You're right.

I did say that we were very focused on improving performance in our Danish business.

It's a very competitive environment there. Both on the household and business banking side, with occasional aggressive pricing moves. From some of our competitors in that market.

We are. Let me take the household first and then the business on the household side. We also suffered from operational issues and other factors. I guess some operational glitches and other issues. That means we haven't been as quick as we are used to in terms of turning around customer decisions and other things. As quick as we are used to in terms of turning around customer decisions and other things. We've taken strong action to address that. And I think the early signs are that we're now very much back in the saddle in terms of providing quick decisions to customers, supporting their home purchases and other things that are important to them.

And then on the business banking side, it's been a very competitive market with some aggressive pricing. And you have to be pragmatic about that. You know, we will pursue good business even if we have to give away a little bit on pricing. But it does mean that occasionally we will walk away from some things. I think we've got a good balance now in terms of winning the business we want to. So I'm pretty confident, and I know Frank Vang-Jensen will want to say something on this, but I'm pretty confident we've got the right formula.

And we'll start to see Denmark improve.

Frank Vang-Jensen

31:28 - 31:55

Yeah, I can only.

Hi, Martin. It's Frank. I can only echo. It's a fine quality.

It's a good business. We want to see more growth, and I think we control that ourselves, and we'll ensure that we do what it takes to make sure that will happen. So all in all, no red flags, but more growth to come.

Martin Ekstedt

31:58 - 32:32

Okay. Understood. Thank you for that clarity.

And then just perhaps a quick one on the deposit hedges.

Did you mention earlier in the presentation that the deposits had contributed positively to the net interest income (NII) during the quarter? But I just wanted to check. Do you mean it had a positive quarter-on-quarter effect? Because if I read the presentation in the back correctly about the impact on NII, it's still negative by 28 million in the quarter, right? And in that case, when would you expect this to turn positive?

Looking at the trajectory, perhaps Q1 26.

Is that a correct read? Thank you.

Ian Smith

32:32 - 33:49

Yeah. So you've picked up correctly the moving parts in Q3.

The deposit hedges are still contributing to dampening the impact of rate cuts. And it will continue to do so as we see rates move down. If we think about Q4, all of the different moving parts mean that Q4 NII will be lower than Q3. There's often a lot of interest as to when the trough in net interest income might occur. And, given the unexpected Riksbank cut recently, it's now sort of is it Q4 this year?

Is it Q1 next year?

But certainly Q4 will be a little bit lower.

The rate reductions are expected to be, in the absence of further rate cuts, probably about 12 basis points of impact in Q4. So that's half of what it was in Q3. The deposit hedged contribution is relatively linear on that basis. So if we've got half the rate cuts, it's probably half the deposit hedge contribution in Q4. I hope that helps.

Martin Ekstedt

33:50 - 33:53

It does.

So all in all, no red flags, but more growth to come. That's all from me.

Operator

33:57 - 34:03

The next question comes from Shree Shrivastava from Citi. Please go ahead.

Shree Shrivastava

34:09 - 34:40

Hi. And thanks very much for taking my questions. I'll keep it short-term given the CMD is happening in about two and a half weeks. First, regarding Treasury Net interest income.

It's actually quite a significant change in the quarter to quarter result. Is this what exactly does this consist of? Does it have to do with timing differences in Sweden or Norway, or is it something else? And I know you don't specifically cite this as a one-off. Could you elaborate on why or why not?

Do you expect this to persist going forward? That's my first question. The next question comes from Shree Shrivastava from Citi.

Ian Smith

34:41 - 35:12

Treasury is quite active in managing funding costs. Quarter on quarter, as you'd expect. That can be slightly opportunistic sometimes. The level you saw in Q3 is, I'd say, probably normal. It's been higher in previous quarters where we've had some specific timing effects. effects. So I think what you're seeing here is active management from Treasury of the funding base. The levels you saw in Q3 are not a bad guide to what we have going forward.

Shree Shrivastava

35:14 - 35:41

The next question comes from Shree Shrivastava from Citi. Thank you very much. And my second question is about these collateral management initiatives that helped RWAs this quarter. I just want to inquire about the timeline, if that's all right. This would point to about 10 billion of RWA benefits.

Is there any timeline in which we can expect these?

Right.

Ian Smith

35:43 - 38:00

So, it's a good question, Trey. So I guess the starting point for this is what we discussed in Q2, which is that as we transition to the full sort of output flow impact, we get closer to standardized risk weights on our IRB portfolios. And as you remember correctly, the pro forma impact of that was reported at around 30 billion; we said 10 billion related to appropriate recognition of collateral on standardized mortgage portfolios. So, that's about a third of the pro forma unmitigated re-inflation due to the output floor and other Basel IV effects. That's something we mentioned regarding the 10 billion mortgage impact that we would work on. The ability to capture the data and use it properly over the next couple of years.

What you've seen in Q3 is the impact of picking up those portfolios that are already standardized and taking advantage of that collateral data. All our other portfolios that, in due course, will be impacted by the output flow. They're all IRB and there isn't anything to be gained at this stage. So we focused on those portfolios that are already standardized. And that drove ten basis points of CET1 improvement in terms of the rest of the aspects. We'll phase that in as the output flow starts to take effect. I don't have a clear timeline yet.

We'll work on that and share it with you. But the main thing is that where we had an advantage or where we had a benefit that could be delivered today, we've focused on that, which is the portfolios that happen to be two key mortgage portfolios in Norway that are on a standardized basis, and we've delivered around a billion of real relief from that.

Shree Shrivastava

38:03 - 38:05

That's very clear.

Thank you very much.

Operator

38:10 - 38:16

The next question comes from Sophie Petersons from Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Sophie Petersons

38:21 - 39:33

Yeah. Hi. Thanks a lot for taking my question. So my first question would be on M&A. We have seen quite a lot of M&A rumors across Europe, but not so much in the Nordics. But if you could maybe just more broadly talk about M&A, how you think about it, how you see the banking landscape in Europe changing and also in the Nordics potentially changing over the next 5 to 10 years.

And how do you think Nordea should be positioned with a five-year view?

If you take into consideration more M&A, more competition, what are you doing to offset this? And then my second question would be around the dividend. I recognize you have the CMD in a couple of weeks' time, but could you maybe just talk about how you expect or how we should think about the potential interim dividend going forward and what the considerations would be for splitting the dividend into an interim and final dividend. Thank you.

Frank Vang-Jensen

39:34 - 39:56

Thank you. This is Frank speaking. I think both are excellent questions for the CMD.

So I'll push them two and a half weeks forward. It's strategic questions and tactical questions.

Both of them.

So I think let's keep them out of this call and then ensure that we have enough time to discuss it when we meet in London in two and a half weeks.

Sophie Petersons

39:57 - 40:29

Okay. Then maybe, if I may ask something different.

So. Regarding the effects we observed, Ross already commented on a decline in profits. Could you just maybe discuss which business units and countries saw the biggest declines in profits? And how should we think about it?

Frank Vang-Jensen

40:29 - 41:57

I think you shouldn't put too much into it. So what we have said all the time is that we, of course, focus a lot on opex and thereby headcounts, and as the year started very much differently than what we had planned due to the trade tariffs, the volatility, the uncertainty, and the geopolitical tension, we knew that this year would be challenged on income. And our response to that, of course, is to first push hard on the income side and the activity level. But secondly, to ensure that the costs are trimmed as well as they can be, with a more operational focus rather than a structural focus. And that is what you see.

So there's no hidden complexities. There's no magic. It's just that the business areas are looking into ensuring that their business is as efficient as they can in the current operational environment. When it comes to what I think you're asking about, it's how it would look in the future. That is one of the topics that we will come back to on Capital Markets Day, which is in two and a half weeks.

And talk about how we see the headcount development and also the cost base in the years to come.

Sophie Petersons

41:59 - 42:03

This is Frank speaking. Okay. Okay. That's clear.

Thank you.

Frank Vang-Jensen

42:03 - 42:03

Thank you.

Operator

42:09 - 42:14

The next question comes from Namita Samtani from Barclays. Please go ahead.

Namita Samtani

42:20 - 43:00

Good morning and thanks for taking my questions.

My first question. Just a hedge contribution on net interest income in 2026.

I notice it's gone up compared to what was previously disclosed. In the second quarter, it increased by 35 million. I was just wondering why that's the case.

And can you help me think about the hedge impact beyond 2026, i.e.

In 2027 and 2028, even if it's just qualitatively?

My second question, I just wonder why Nordea is not part of the nine European banks that are going to launch a euro-denominated stablecoin. And I just wondered what your plans are with stablecoins going forward? Thanks.

Ian Smith

43:02 - 45:09

Good morning, and thanks for your questions.

Yes. We've slightly tweaked our hedge volumes. As you can see on slide 17, we're always alert to opportunities to manage our exposure and sensitivity. And that means we've kind of lowered the overall estimate of sensitivity slightly. That has the impact of, certainly in the current environment of rates coming down, helping a little bit with the start of 2026. And we've also seen, as I said before, an unexpected Riksbank cut.

In an expected environment of stable rates thereafter, we would then expect to see stability in terms of hedge impact on NII.

So, you know, we always said that 2025 and a little bit into 2026, you'd see some help from the hedge and stability thereafter.

That remains how we think about it.

And then your second question, just on the initiatives that other banks have banded together to look at stablecoin, it's certainly an interesting initiative. We talk to those other banks fairly regularly about how they're thinking about it, and they have made it clear that they're open to other banks joining that initiative in due course. We have a lot of different options that we're looking at and working on regarding the payment side. And if that were to be relevant for us, we would look at it pretty closely.

I think it's overall a pretty positive initiative. I think there are plenty of options that might turn out to be better than a digital currency for the euro and solve the issues that the ECB is trying to solve with its digital currency.

So we'll keep a close eye on that.

Namita Samtani

45:11 - 45:13

That's helpful.

Thanks very much.

Operator

45:19 - 45:25

The next question comes from Gulnara Silva from Morgan Stanley.

Please go ahead.
